description: Food provenance, food miles, packaging trade-offs, sustainability of food choices, food poverty and food security.
content_html:
Where Does Your Food Come From?

Food provenance is about knowing the origin and journey of the food on your plate. A Sunday roast in a home kitchen might involve lamb from Wales, potatoes from Lincolnshire, green beans flown from Kenya and olive oil pressed in Italy. Each ingredient has a story — where it was grown, reared or caught, and how far it travelled before it arrived on the supermarket shelf.

Foods can be grown, reared or caught. Vegetables and cereals are grown in soil; livestock (cattle, sheep, pigs) are reared on farms; fish and shellfish are caught wild from rivers and seas or farmed in aquaculture systems. Understanding the origin of food matters for three reasons: it affects the nutritional quality and freshness of what we eat, it has environmental consequences (in terms of land use, water and energy), and it raises ethical questions about animal welfare, worker conditions and fair trade.

Food Miles and Carbon Footprint

Food miles measure the distance food travels from origin to consumer. A punnet of strawberries grown in a Kent field and sold in a local farm shop has very few food miles. A punnet of strawberries airfreighted from Peru to a supermarket distribution centre and then transported by lorry to a suburban store has thousands. Food miles contribute to a product’s carbon footprint, because transporting food by lorry, ship or air burns fossil fuels and releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.

However, food miles are not the only measure of environmental impact. A tomato grown in a heated greenhouse in the UK in January can have a higher carbon footprint than a tomato grown in the Spanish sun and transported by ship, because the energy needed to heat the UK greenhouse year-round is substantial. The relationship between food miles and environmental impact is therefore not straightforward, and a fuller analysis must consider growing method, energy use and packaging alongside transport distance.

Buying locally often does reduce food miles — and supporting local producers has real economic and community benefits. But ‘local’ does not automatically mean ‘low carbon’. A heated UK polytunnel growing tomatoes in December uses significant energy. Seasonal, local food (British strawberries in June; British root vegetables in winter) genuinely has a lower environmental footprint than the same product airfreighted out of season. The key is to combine local sourcing with seasonal eating — the two together give the biggest environmental benefit.

The Impact of Packaging

Packaging has both costs and benefits. On the negative side, single-use plastic packaging generates waste that can persist in landfill and oceans for hundreds of years. Packaging production consumes energy and raw materials. Excessive packaging — a single cucumber wrapped tightly in plastic, a tray of four apples enclosed in a plastic box — is widely criticised for adding environmental cost with little benefit.

On the positive side, packaging plays a genuine food-safety role. Modified atmosphere packaging (MAP) — where the air inside a packet is replaced with a gas mix that slows oxidation and bacterial growth — can extend the shelf life of fresh meat by several days, reducing the amount that spoils before it can be eaten. Vacuum-sealed and airtight packaging reduces food waste in transit. Without packaging, far more food would be damaged, contaminated or wasted during transport and storage. The environmental question is not simply “packaging or no packaging” but rather “what is the minimum packaging necessary to safely deliver the food to the consumer?”

Sustainability of Food

Sustainability in food production means meeting today’s food needs without degrading the resources — land, water, biodiversity — that future generations will need. It encompasses farming practices (intensive vs organic, monoculture vs rotation), fishing methods (trawling vs line-caught), land use change (deforestation for soya and palm oil), water consumption and waste management.

Food waste itself is a major sustainability problem. When food is wasted, all the land, water, energy and labour that went into producing it is also wasted — and then further emissions are generated when the food decomposes in landfill. In the UK, households throw away approximately 6.7 million tonnes of food every year, much of it perfectly edible. The environmental, economic and social costs of this waste ripple outwards: higher food prices for all consumers, increased pressure on agricultural land, and greater greenhouse gas emissions. Reducing food waste — through better meal planning, correct storage, and using leftovers — is one of the most impactful individual actions a household can take.

Key Fact

Food waste creates three types of harm: environmental (greenhouse gas emissions, wasted land and water), economic (higher costs to producers and consumers) and social (food discarded while others go hungry). Reducing food waste is one of the most direct ways an individual can improve the sustainability of their food choices.

Food Poverty and Food Security

These two terms are closely related but have distinct meanings. Food poverty operates at the household and individual level: it describes the situation of a family that cannot afford to buy enough food, or cannot access nutritious food because there are no affordable shops nearby, or must choose between eating and paying heating bills. Food poverty in the UK has grown in recent years; food banks report record numbers of referrals.

Food security, as defined by the World Health Organisation (WHO), operates at a global level. It is achieved when all people, at all times, have physical and economic access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food. Food insecurity — the absence of food security — can result from conflict, drought, crop failure, price volatility, trade disruption and poverty. Around 735 million people globally were experiencing hunger as of recent WHO estimates, despite the world producing enough food calories to feed everyone.

Food poverty and food insecurity are therefore not the same: a person can be food-insecure in a wealthy country (unable to afford nutritious food despite food being physically available), or food-secure in a lower-income country (where subsistence farming provides reliable nutrition). The distinction matters in exam answers — using both terms precisely signals sophisticated understanding.

Key Fact

Food poverty = individuals or households unable to afford or access a healthy diet (household/individual scale). Food security = all people at all times having physical and economic access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food (global scale — World Health Organisation definition). These are distinct terms — do not use them interchangeably in your exam.

In everyday conversation, the two terms are often used as synonyms — but your exam uses them with specific technical meanings derived from the spec. Food poverty is about affordability and access at the individual or household level. Food security is about the reliability and safety of the food supply for all people globally, as defined by the World Health Organisation. A top-band exam answer would define both terms, explain how they relate to each other (food poverty is a cause of food insecurity; addressing food insecurity requires tackling food poverty among other factors), and apply both to a named context or population group.
exam_tip_html: This lesson’s capstone is the 12-mark Evaluate — the highest-tariff question on the paper. The command word definition is “make a reasoned qualitative judgement, weighing strengths and weaknesses against a clear criterion.” The most common mistake on 12-mark Evaluate questions is to describe rather than evaluate: listing the pros and cons of local vs imported food without ever reaching a supported judgement. Top-band responses weigh the evidence (“local, seasonal food is the stronger environmental choice because… however, the picture is complicated by…”) and conclude with a reasoned position. You do not need to agree with a particular view — you need to show you have considered both sides and can justify which is the stronger argument for the stated context. Anchor your judgement to the named eater or scenario in the question. Use technical vocabulary: food miles, carbon footprint, water activity, food security, sustainability.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Food provenance covers where and how food is grown, reared or caught. Food miles measure transport distance, but a fuller environmental picture must also consider growing method, energy use and packaging — local is not always lower-carbon.
  • Packaging has both costs (waste, energy in production) and benefits (reduces spoilage, extends shelf life, protects food safety). The aim is minimum necessary packaging rather than no packaging at all.
  • Food poverty (household inability to afford a healthy diet) and food security (global access to sufficient, safe, nutritious food — WHO definition) are distinct terms with distinct meanings. Food waste has environmental, economic and social costs and reducing it is one of the most impactful individual sustainability actions.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes 'food miles'?
A) The total weight of food transported by road each year
B) The distance food travels from where it is produced to where it is eaten
C) The number of calories burned walking to the supermarket
D) The financial cost of importing food from overseas
practice_questions.marks: B) The distance food travels from where it is produced to where it is eaten [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two ways in which food waste has a negative impact on the environment.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for each of two distinct environmental impacts (up to 2 marks):
- Food waste decomposing in landfill produces methane, a potent greenhouse gas that contributes to climate change.
- All the land, water and energy used to produce the wasted food is also wasted — increasing pressure on agricultural land and water resources.
- Transport involved in producing and delivering food that is then wasted generates unnecessary carbon dioxide emissions.
- Food waste in landfill can produce leachate that contaminates soil and groundwater.

practice_questions.text: Describe the World Health Organisation's definition of food security.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks for an accurate description:
- Food security exists when all people (1) at all times (1) have physical and economic access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food to meet their dietary needs for an active and healthy life (1).
Candidates who give a partial definition (e.g. 'enough food for everyone') score 1 mark. Full marks require all three elements: universality (all people), reliability (at all times), and sufficiency/safety/nutritional quality.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between food poverty and food security, giving one cause of each.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark per developed point, up to 4 marks:
- Food poverty is the inability of individuals or households to afford or access a healthy, nutritious diet — caused by factors such as low income, unemployment or high food prices relative to other living costs (1 mark for definition + 1 mark for a named cause).
- Food security is the global condition in which all people at all times have physical and economic access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food (WHO definition) — insecurity can be caused by conflict, drought, crop failure, trade disruption or price volatility (1 mark for definition + 1 mark for a named cause).
Candidates who use the two terms synonymously score a maximum of 1 mark.

practice_questions.text:
A family is deciding whether to buy vegetables from a local farm shop or from a supermarket that sources produce from overseas.

Evaluate the environmental and social impact of buying locally produced food versus imported food. In your answer, consider the advantages and disadvantages of each choice and reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10–12 marks): Arguments for local sourcing (reduced food miles, lower transport emissions, supports local economy and communities, fresher produce with potentially higher nutrient retention) presented with development and specific examples. Arguments against (local heated-greenhouse production may have a higher carbon footprint out of season; local supply chains can be less reliable; imported food may be grown more efficiently in better-suited climates; seasonal restriction limits dietary variety). Weighing of evidence is explicit — not just listing pros and cons. A supported judgement is present and anchored to the context: e.g. 'For a family buying seasonal British vegetables in summer, local sourcing offers genuine environmental benefits with few trade-offs; however, in winter, the picture is more complex because...' Technical vocabulary used: food miles, carbon footprint, sustainability, food security, food poverty.

Secure (7–9 marks): Both sides of the argument presented and most points developed. Some technical vocabulary. Judgement present but weighing of evidence is partial — one side more fully developed than the other.

Developing (4–6 marks): Both sides mentioned but mostly descriptive. Limited development of reasons. Technical vocabulary sparse. Judgement may be present but is not fully supported by the argument.

Emerging (1–3 marks): One-sided argument or a list of facts. No judgement. Basic vocabulary.

practice_questions.text: Identify one benefit and one drawback of packaging for fresh food products.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for a distinct benefit and 1 mark for a distinct drawback (up to 2 marks):
- Benefit: packaging protects food from contamination; extends shelf life by reducing oxygen exposure or preventing physical damage; reduces food waste in transit.
- Drawback: single-use plastic packaging generates waste that persists in landfill and oceans; packaging production consumes energy and raw materials; excessive packaging adds environmental cost with little benefit.

knowledge_checks.q: Which organisation provides the widely used definition of food security ('all people at all times have physical and economic access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food')?
Food _____ describes the inability of individuals or households to afford or access a healthy, nutritious diet.
The total amount of greenhouse gases produced by a food product from origin to consumer is called its _____.
Match each term to its definition:
right: The distance food travels from where it is produced to where it is eaten
The global condition in which all people at all times have access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food
Meeting present food needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs

flashcard_questions.a: Knowledge of where a food was grown, reared or caught, and the journey it made to the consumer.
The distance food travels from where it is produced to where it is eaten.
The total greenhouse gases produced directly and indirectly by a product, expressed in CO2 equivalent.

flashcard_questions.q: Why are food miles not the only measure of a food's environmental impact?
flashcard_questions.a: Growing method and energy use (e.g. heated greenhouses) can make local food higher carbon than imported food.
The inability of individuals or households to afford or access a healthy, nutritious diet.
When all people at all times have physical and economic access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food.

flashcard_questions.q: What is sustainability in food production?
flashcard_questions.a: Meeting present food needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.

flashcard_questions.q: Give two environmental impacts of food waste.
flashcard_questions.a: Methane emissions from landfill decomposition; wasted land, water and energy used in production.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one benefit of packaging for food products.
flashcard_questions.a: Modified atmosphere packaging extends shelf life by slowing oxidation and bacterial growth.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one drawback of packaging for food products.
flashcard_questions.a: Single-use plastic generates long-lasting waste in landfill and oceans.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the key difference between food poverty and food security?
flashcard_questions.a: Food poverty is at household level; food security is a global concept defined by the WHO.

flashcard_questions.q: How does buying seasonal, locally grown food reduce environmental impact?
flashcard_questions.a: It reduces food miles and avoids the energy cost of heated greenhouses growing out-of-season produce.

glossary_terms.definition: Knowledge of where a food was grown, reared or caught, including its country of origin, farming method and the journey it made to reach the consumer.
The distance food travels from where it is grown or produced to where it is eaten, used as a measure of the environmental impact of a food product.
The total amount of greenhouse gases produced directly and indirectly by an activity, product or organisation, expressed in tonnes of CO2 equivalent.
The ability to produce food in a way that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
The inability of individuals or households to afford or access a healthy, nutritious diet, often as a result of low income, unemployment or high food prices.

As defined by the World Health Organisation: the condition in which all people at all times have physical and economic access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food to meet their dietary needs for an active and healthy life.
Food that is discarded or not eaten, causing environmental harm through methane emissions in landfill and wasting the land, water and energy used in its production.

hero_image_caption: Knowing where food comes from — and how far it has travelled — helps us make more sustainable food choices.
